tagline: A long, narrow valley links Pikeville, Dunlap, Whitwell and Jasper
intro: The Sequatchie Valley National Scenic Byway follows a rolling valley bordered by mountains, a 70-mile drive in the byway organization’s description. The valley itself is almost perfectly straight, with a width of about three to five miles. Tennessee’s Department of Transportation identifies scenic and recreational qualities as the basis for this National Scenic Byway, emphasizing the landscape and opportunities for hiking, fishing and wildlife watching. The byway organization describes curves and overlooks along the route; the straightness belongs to the valley, not to every mile of highway.

Travel through the valley mattered before the present highway. During the Civil War, a rough route through it supplied the Union army at Chattanooga. At Crossville, a branch of the Great Stage Road met the Kentucky Stock Road, a cattle-driving route that eventually extended south to Chattanooga. Those roads were widened, improved and paved; U.S. 70 and U.S. 127 now roughly follow the old routes.

Drive north from Jasper on TN 28 through Whitwell to Dunlap, then continue on U.S. 127 toward Pikeville. At Dunlap, the coke ovens lie at the foot of Fredonia Mountain west of downtown. Beyond Pikeville, U.S. 127 climbs toward Crossville on the plateau. The driving itinerary finishes at I-40 in Crossville.

moments.title: Whitwell
moments.text: A German transport railcar surrounded by a small garden forms Whitwell’s Children’s Holocaust Memorial. Its 11 million paper clips grew out of a school project begun in 1998. Principal Linda M. Hooper asked for an after-school project to teach tolerance, and David Smith and Sandra Roberts developed a Holocaust education program. Students sought objects that could represent lives lost in the Holocaust, choosing paper clips after researching Norwegian resistance to Nazi occupation. The memorial was unveiled on November 9, 2001, the anniversary of Kristallnacht. The railcar is located at Whitwell Middle School.

moments.title: Dunlap Coke Ovens
moments.text: Five batteries of 268 beehive ovens remain at Dunlap’s former coke works. Coal from Fredonia Mountain traveled down an incline railway and into openings atop the ovens. Workers heated it in closed chambers to remove volatile material, producing coke for Chattanooga’s iron furnaces. The ovens have sandstone exteriors and firebrick interiors. Volunteers helped clear the abandoned site before the park opened in 1987. Its museum occupies a reconstructed commissary on the original foundation, and a trail follows the incline railway’s grade toward the former mines. The ruins of the 1906 coal washer are also part of the park.

moments.title: Pikeville
moments.text: Pikeville’s Old Town Spring supplied the town’s main water source until 1920 and remains visible. The town was established in 1816, and the Bledsoe County seat moved here from Madison by 1818. U.S. 127 runs through its business district and courthouse square, with a bypass through the newer commercial area to the west. North of town, the highway rises up the mountain near the county line. Tom Wigle helped build that stretch during a summer job between semesters at Vanderbilt’s engineering school. The Sequatchie River passes through the eastern section of town.
